title: The girl from the furrow
hook: a king is plowing a field, and a girl rises out of the furrow
carry: sita is earth's daughter, and the earth is mother

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a season with the breath again: Bhrigu found that breath is Brahman, and learned the self lies deeper still.

A king is plowing. Not a farmer, a king, walking behind the plow, clearing a field. And out of the furrow, out of the turned earth, a girl rises. He lifts her up, takes her home, and raises her as his own daughter. The king is Janaka of Mithila. The girl is Sita. A new season starts today: the women of the epics, heard in their own words where the texts give them words. It starts with the one who came out of the ground.
screen: `A KING BEHIND THE PLOW.` → `A GIRL RISES FROM THE FURROW.` → `A SEASON OF THE EPICS' WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The story comes late in the first book of Valmiki's Ramayana, from Janaka's own mouth. In paraphrase: while I was plowing the field, a girl rose from the earth. I found her while clearing the ground, and she is known by the name Sita. She was not born from a womb, he adds, and he calls her his daughter. Then he sets a test for her suitors: string the great bow of Shiva. In the next chapter, Rama lifts it, and it breaks. Three things to hold as this season begins. First, the name. Tradition hears in it the Sanskrit word for a furrow, the line the plow cuts. Second, her father. The Upanishads tell of a King Janaka who loved to ask about the self, the one heard earlier on this path questioning Yajnavalkya, and tradition links Sita's father to that king or his line. Third, the shape of her story. She comes out of the earth at the start, and in the Ramayana's last book the ground opens and takes her home. That's why Hindus call her Bhumija, born of the earth, and it rests on a teaching older than her story: the earth is a goddess and a mother, Bhudevi. Many Hindus still say a short prayer in the morning before their feet touch the floor, asking Mother Earth to forgive them for stepping on her. The season ahead follows Sita's own words and choices. It starts with the ground under everyone's feet.
screen: `JANAKA TELLS IT IN HIS OWN WORDS` · `A NAME THAT CARRIES THE FIELD` · `FROM THE EARTH, AND BACK TO IT` · `BHUDEVI: THE EARTH AS MOTHER`

segments.voice: Let your weight drop and notice exactly where the floor or the earth meets you, the feet, the seat, the hands, settling a little more with each breath out onto the same ground that was under Sita, turned, planted, walked on. If you pray, you can greet the earth as a mother, as many Hindus do before stepping down in the morning; otherwise, simply rest on it with thanks.
Sita. In Valmiki, Janaka finds her rising from the earth as he plows, and tradition hears the furrow in her name. Today's word.
Your line: Sita is earth's daughter, and the earth is mother. From the furrow at the start, and back to the earth at the end. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sita is honored in Hindu devotion as a goddess and as Rama's wife, called Bhumija, born of the earth; her birth is celebrated in some communities as Sita Navami, and many Hindus greet the earth, Bhudevi, with a short prayer before stepping down in the morning.
